column2: Those two, the experience of pleasure and pain, which produce the body and the rest, arise from dharma and adharma; the creature obtains a body and so on in order to enjoy.
Dharma and adharma are the cause everywhere for every creature, O king; so why ask for a cause beyond them?
The king said: "There is no doubt that dharma and adharma are the cause in all effects, and the passing from body to body is for enjoyment.
But what you said, that 'who I am' cannot be told of the Self — I wish to hear that.
O Brahmin, how can one who exists not say 'I'? The word 'I', applied to the Self itself, is no fault, O twice-born."
The Brahmin said: "The word 'I' is no fault in the Self itself, nor is it so in that way; but the notion of self in what is not the self, or the word, is marked as scriptural error.
The tongue says 'I', O king, as do the teeth, lips and palate; but I am not these, since all are only causes of producing speech.
What use are the causes? Speech itself says 'I am speech' — yet it is not right for speech to say 'I' in that way.
Since the body of a man, marked by head, hands and so on, is separate, then to what, O king, do I apply this name 'I'?
If there were another, superior to me, O best of kings, then 'I am not the body; this is another' could be said.
When the one Person abides in all bodies, then the words 'Who are you? Who am I?' are fruitless.
You are the king, this is the palanquin, we are the bearers going before; and this is your world — but that, O king, is not true.
From the tree comes wood, and from it this palanquin on which you sit. Where is the name 'tree' for it, or 'wood', O king?
The great king seated on the tree is not spoken of so by your people; nor does everyone call you 'wood' when you are in the palanquin.
The palanquin is an assembly of wooden parts held in its own arrangement; O best of kings, look for the palanquin apart from them.
So consider the umbrella as separate from its ribs: where is the umbrella born? The same reasoning applies to you and to me.
'Man, woman, cow, goat, horse, elephant, bird, tree' — this is the worldly naming of bodies, to be understood as due to karma.
The Person is not a god, not a man, not an animal, not a tree; these varieties of bodily shape, O king, are born of karma.
What in the world is called 'king' and what consists of the king's soldiers, and so with the other, O king, is not true; it is made of imagination.
That which, even after a time, reaches the name of destruction, born of transformation and the like — what is that thing, O king?
You are king of all the world, son of your father, enemy of your enemy, husband of your wife, father of your son: what shall I call you, O king?
Are you this head? Are you the belly? Are you the feet and the rest? None of this is yours, O lord of the earth.
You stand apart from all the limbs. Becoming expert, reflect here, O king: 'Who am I?'
When the truth is so established, how can 'I' be thought of by me, accomplished by separate utterance, O king?"
Knowledge is the highest truth; the one who sees non-falsely knows it. By the divisions of the holes of the flute, the differences called shadja and so on arise.
There is no difference in the all-pervading wind, and so too of that Great Soul. Oneness and the differences of form arise from the activities of outward action.
He is established amid the differences of gods and the rest, and yet has no conduct. Hear here, O king, the earlier account sung by Ribhu.
Ribhu, the son of Brahma the Supreme, was the one who awakened the twice-born Nidagha.
Knowing the truth by nature itself, O king, he had formerly a disciple Nidagha, son of Pulastya.
He gave him all knowledge with great joy; but Nidagha, though he gained knowledge of the truth, did not have the impression of non-duality.
Ribhu thought of Nidagha, O king: on the bank of the Devika was a city named Nagara,
prosperous and very lovely, founded by Pulastya, ending in pleasant groves; there, O best of kings,
the knower of yoga named Nidagha had formerly been his disciple. After a divine thousand years had passed, Ribhu
went to that city to see his disciple Nidagha. At the time of the Vaishvadeva offering, he came into view at the door.
Nidagha, standing there and taking his purpose, brought him into his own house, washed his hands and feet, and gave him a seat.
That best of Brahmins said respectfully, "Please eat." Ribhu said: "O best of Brahmins, what food is there in your house to eat?
Tell me; I have no liking for poor food." Nidagha said: "In my house are barley-meal, gruel, rice and cakes;
whatever you like, O best of Brahmins, eat as you wish." Ribhu said: "These are poor foods, O Brahmin; give me sweet food,
preparations of rice and milk and so on, and sugar-cane juicy things." Nidagha said: "In my house, O householder's wife, whatever is delightful,
among foods the sweet is a means; prepare his food with that." Told so by him, his wife, out of respect for her husband's word,
prepared that sweet food for the Brahmin. The great sage ate it, not from desire.
Nidagha, standing bowed with humility, said, O king: "Has supreme satisfaction arisen in you, and nourishment?
Has your mind been made at ease by the food, O Brahmin? Where do you live, O Brahmin, and where are you set to go?
Whence have you come? Please tell me." Ribhu said: "For a hungry man who has eaten, O Brahmin, satisfaction arises.
I have no hunger to be satisfied; why do you ask me, O Brahmin? When burned first by fire and earth, hunger takes hold.
And when water is spent, thirst arises in men. Hunger and thirst are called properties of the body; they are not mine, O Brahmin.
Therefore, since hunger does not arise, I am always satisfied. Calmness of mind and contentment are properties of the mind, O Brahmin.
Whatever was asked of the mind — a person is not joined with these. 'Where do you live?' and 'Where will you go?' that you said,
and 'whence do you come?' — hear me on these three too. This Person is all-going, pervading like space;
how then is 'whence, where, to where will you go' meaningful? I am he: neither goer nor non-goer, not dwelling in one place.
You and others — not you, you; not others, nor am I I. 'Sweet food' as 'sweet' — this tongue of mine was made by you;
what will it say? Hear that too, O best of Brahmins: what is sweet is itself what is unpleasant, the cause of distress.
The unpleasant becomes sweet; people are disgusted by the sweet. In the beginning, middle and end, what food is the cause of taste?
As a clay house plastered with clay becomes firm, so this body is earthy, made of earthy atoms.
Barley, wheat, mung, ghee, oil, milk, curd, jaggery and fruit — so too are earthy atoms.
Knowing this, you who discriminate sweet and unpleasant: that mind should be quieted and made fit for liberation."
Hearing his words based on the highest truth, O king, the fortunate Nidagha bowed and said:
Be gracious for my benefit; tell me who you are who has come. My delusion is gone on hearing these words, O Brahmin.
Ribhu said: "I am Ribhu, your teacher, come here to give you wisdom, O Brahmin; I shall give you the well-taught highest truth.
Know this as one; the whole world has no difference. It is the nature of the Supreme Self, named Vasudeva."
The Brahmin said: "So be it," said Nidagha; honoured with supreme devotion after prostrating, the Lord went away, though unwilling to be detained.
After a thousand years, O king, the teacher came again to that city to give Nidagha knowledge.
Outside the city he saw the sage Nidagha, as the king was entering the city with a great retinue,
standing far off, O fortunate one, avoiding the crush of people, his throat wasted with hunger, coming from the forest with firewood and kusha.
Seeing Nidagha, Ribhu approached and greeted him and said: "Why do you stand apart, O Brahmin?"
Nidagha said: "O sage, there is a great crowd of people here with the lord of the people; as he wishes to enter the lovely city, I stand here."
Ribhu said: "Who is the king here and who are the other people? Tell me, O best of Brahmins; you are held by me to be knowing."
Nidagha said: "The one who has mounted the mad elephant, huge as a mountain peak, is the king; and the others around are his retinue."
Ribhu said: "I have seen these two, elephant and king, at once; you have shown them separately, as marked by the Vedas without distinction.
So tell me, O fortunate one, the distinction between these two; I wish to know which is the elephant and which the king."
Nidagha said: "The one below, Brahmin, is the elephant; above him is the king. Who does not know the relation of carried and carrier, O Brahmin?"
Ribhu said: "Brahmin, make me understand as I might know: what is the division of 'below' and what is called 'above'?"
The Brahmin said: Having said so, Nidagha quickly climbed up and said to Ribhu: "Take refuge; I tell you what you ask me.
I am above like the king, you below like the elephant. For your understanding, Brahmin, I have shown you the example."
Ribhu said: "O best of Brahmins, if you are like the king and I stand like the elephant, then tell me: which are you and which am I?"
The Brahmin said: Thus addressed, he quickly bowed at his feet, and Nidagha said: "Lord, you are my teacher Ribhu.
The mind refined by the impressions of duality is not otherwise, like the teacher's; so I take you as the guru I have attained."
Ribhu said: "To give you instruction, from your earlier service and love for the teacher, I, Ribhu, came to Nidagha.
That has been taught to you in brief, O great-minded one: the essence of the highest truth, non-duality in full."
The Brahmin said: Having said so, the teacher Ribhu gave Nidagha the knowledge; and Nidagha by that teaching became devoted to non-duality.
He saw all beings without difference in himself, and so the twice-born attained supreme liberation in the form of Brahman.
So you too, knower of dharma, equal toward self, foe and kinsman, become all-pervading knowledge, O lord of the earth, the Self.
As the one sky is seen as white, blue and so on, so the Self, to deluded eyes, appears one and many.
Whatever there is here is the one Achyuta; there is nothing else higher than him. I am he, you are he, all this is he: the Self shines by itself, free of the delusion of difference.
Sanandana said: Thus told by him, the best of kings gave up difference, with sight of the highest truth; and awakened by memory of his births, attained liberation in that very birth.
This highest truth of the Self has been told to you, O lord of sages; it gives liberation even to Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and listeners.
As you asked, O Brahmin, so it has been told by me. This is pure knowledge of Brahman; what else shall I tell?
Pishachas, asuras and rakshasas live by a low tone; the world of moving and unmoving things by an extremely low pitch.
All beings are indeed sustained by tones in the Sama; of the bright, long, pitiful, soft and middle...
He who knows the distinctions of the shrutis (micro-tones) is not called a teacher otherwise. The bright in the low, in the second, and also in the fourth,
in the extra-high and in the third; in the cry the pitiful shruti. The shrutis of the second tone are held to be soft, middle and long.
I shall tell their characteristics separately: length in the low, softness in the opposite;
in one's own tone, middleness — having observed that one should apply it. In the second, what is paused, and the cry follows;
that is to be known as bright; softness is by the first. Here too what is paused is carried by the fourth;
so in the low it should be bright at the conclusion of the Sama. He should not make an excessively high shruti between two tones.
Nor in the short, in the long, or in the one called ghuti. The movement is twofold: the junction of word-end with the sibilants.
In these five places the ghuti is to be known; the pauses between tones, the short, the long, and the ghuti;
in the rest of the stations one should speak in tone like a shruti. The bright is known in the udatta, and the bright in the svarita.
In the anudatta, soft; the Gandharvas for the perfection of shruti. Udatta, anudatta, svarita, pracita,
and nighata — the tone-differences are to be known as fivefold. Beyond this I shall tell the three tones of the teaching.
Udatta, anudatta and third svarita tone. What is called udatta, that is the one before the svarita;
the knowers call it pracaya; there is no other tone here. The syllable-tone and the past tone are the twofold svarita.
The measure-bearing syllable is thus long after the uttered; it is to be known as sevenfold by seeing the suffix.
It is to be known by the word, according to where it stands. One should use the seven tones in regard to the right ear.
The treatise was composed by the teachers wishing the good of sons and pupils. There is nothing higher than the high, nor lower than the low.
In the name vaisvarya-svara, what station is called svara? Between the high and low is the common one, as the shruti says.
The phonologists know that svara in the name svara; in the udatta, nishada and gandhara; in the anudatta, rishabha and dhaivata;
these, born of the svarita, are shadja, madhyama and panchama. Where the sibilants after ka and kha serve at the root of the tongue,
they should also be ordered by measure; by nature that is the digit. Jatya, kshaipra, abhinihita, tairovyanjana,
tirovirama, prashlishta and the seventh, padavritta — I shall tell the separate characteristic of these tones,
and the rule and example of those listed. A syllable with "pa" or "va" becomes svarita;
one before which there is no udatta is called jatya svara. When "i" and "u" sounds, being udatta, sometimes come to "pa" and "va"...
know that the mark of kshaipra is the anudatta in the suffix. The "a" that is placed in "e" and "o", both udatta,
where the "a" disappears, they call that abhinihita. Whatever is svarita in metre after an udatta
is called "many-toned", tairovyanjana. Where a svarita follows immediately after an avagraha,
know that as tirovirama if the avagraha is udatta. Where one sees "i" joined with "i" only,
consider that prashlishta: udatta joined to anudatta. If svarita, where open and where combined (samhita),
this is the mark of padavritta as taught in the treatise. The other svara, the jatya one, is called kshaipra before the shruti.
... for protection; tirovirama in the shifted; prashlishta, the "ee" sound...
padavritta ... the seven tones begin so. Whatever syllable the tone is on before the one syllable...
this is called the natural form of svaras apart from jatya. The first four svaras are by the treatise on kampa, shapha, pum, sphuti.
In the udatta and the single low, "juhvo 'gnih" is an example. A short "i" ending a word, with "u" following,
the wise one knows the short kampa, without doubt. And with "i" ending a word and two "u"s in the next word,
know the long kampa — "shag-dhushu" is the example. Three long ones are to be known which are in the diphthongs:
manya yatha na indrabhyam — the rest are called short. If many udattas have an anudatta suffix...
know "shivakampa" if the suffix is udatta. Where there are two or more udatta syllables,
the wise know the udatta where a low or high follows. No doubling occurs sometimes in "r" or "h",
nor in the second letters of the classes, nor ever in the fourth: the fourth with the third, the second with the first.
The first, last and middle should be pressed by the svara syllable. If the first is not final and the last follows...
there between, the yama stands, of its own class from the preceding letters. Seeing the class-final letters joined with sibilants or semivowels,
the yamas turn back like travellers without a guide. The third and fourth; a word beginning with the fourth;
two thirds and "h"; a word beginning with "h"; anusvara, upadhmaniya and jihvamuliya, sometimes in order after.
In joining with "r" and "h" before, the later syllable proceeds. Where a conjunct is seen, a consonant in a final word,
having made the first part from the beginning, he should place it at the start of the latter part. Where there is a svarita in a conjunct, udvata, and pratana,
know that as the former part, where the start is made, the other is the latter. From the conjunct, know the latter as leading the conjunct;
of a conjunct consonant, the following is the preceding syllable. Anusvara and the word-end by sequence in its own suffix;
svarabhakti and "r" are said to be the former part, each in turn. At the start of a foot or not the start, in conjuncts and avagrahas,
the word "ya" is to be known as the other "saya". At the start of a foot and in non-separation, standing at the end of conjuncts,
except for "r" and "h", the instruction is seen. A syllable joined with its own is heavy; with anusvara it is plain...
What is udatta stays udatta; what is svarita, in the word it remains; what is low remains low; what stands in pracaya is also low.
Agnih, "sutah", "mitram idam", "vayam", "ayavahah", "priyam", "dutam", "ghritam", "chittam" — the word "ati" is low.
In "akveshu eva", "suteshu eva", in sacrifices and pots, in hundreds with purifiers, the shruti is uttered from low to high.
In "Hari", "Varuna", "Vareniya", "Dhara", "Purusha", the svarabhakti "r"; "Vishvanara" with "n"; the rest are svarita.

The two Varunas, "vasvarata", "uduttamam tva Varuna", "dhara", "urudharamurudhare"... a syllable one-mora or two-mora in sound: its start is half a mora, the rest comes after. A short is to be made like a long; the doubly toned is used so.
Kampa, sung svarita, and short-drawing; a mora is the time of a wink, others say the time of lightning.
Or the Rik tone is said by some as having equal union.
In a compound one should make the avagraha, and the word connected here; the "yeti" and "akshara" and the like are of the end of a word, so they know.

(Everywhere the words mitra, putra, sakhi, ahi, shatakratu are to be separated; Aditya, vipra, jatavedas, satpati, gopati, vritrahan, samudra, ... ) and the wise do not separate "chikiti" and "dha"; I hold that there are four open (vivrita) vowels.
By the order of syllables hear their names from me: the short and the like, "vatsanusrita", and "vatsanusarini" first;
pakavati, the short, the long, "vriddha" and "pipilika" — the interval of the four vivritis is one mora.
